sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Xipe** (*xipe*) — Spring, Agriculture, Flayed · The flayed one — belongs to the Nahuatl tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Spring, Agriculture, Flayed". The name means "The flayed one".

**Xipe** is spring, agriculture, flayed. The name means "The flayed one" and belongs to the nahuatl tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Xipe** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/xipe/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *xipe* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in the colonial alphabetic corpus and in logographic writing in the codices; the restoration uses the normalized scholarly orthography. Etymologically the name means "The flayed one".

The ASCII form *xipe* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Xipe** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **x** → **X** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **p** → **p** — Same
- **e** → **e** — Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/xipe/** — Restored scholarly form.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **xipe** — The canonical restored form Xipe.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Say "xipe" with the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Xipe".

The ASCII form "xipe" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Xipe" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation given above reconstructs the sound world in which Xipe was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The restoration Xipe keeps the prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual nahuatl names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.

The form **Xipe** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of Xipe place spring, agriculture, flayed at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Xipe appears in nahuatl tradition as spring, agriculture, flayed. The name's meaning, "The flayed one", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Xipe in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Xipe survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Xipe gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Xipe remains a touchstone for understanding nahuatl religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Xipe includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Xipe remains findable and citable.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Xipe with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Nahuatl name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Xipe, sanctuary or cult remains tied to spring and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

sections.label: Florentine Codex
sections.body:
Bernardino de Sahagún's Florentine Codex, compiled in sixteenth-century Mexico, records Xipe in Nahuatl and Spanish. The twelve books cover gods, rituals, natural history, and society, preserving Aztec voices through colonial mediation.

The restored form Xipe follows normalized Nahuatl orthography.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
To contemplate Xipe is to hold the idea of spring, Agriculture, Flayed in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "The flayed one" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as spring, Agriculture, Flayed · The flayed one.

Sit with the restored form — Xipe — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form *xipe* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.
